name: WILLIS LEASE FINANCE

priced.reason: not a repriceable fcff name or no growth supplied

devils_advocate.strongest_counter: The counter to declaring this unmodellable is that WLFC is not a bank — it owns hard assets with observable residual values, reports EBIT and interest expense cleanly, and a normal FCFF model ought to handle a lessor the same way it handles a railroad or a shipping company. On that view I should fix the capex input rather than abandon the model, and the answer would be that a business earning $114M of net income on $662M of equity, marked at $1.1B of market capitalisation, is not obviously mispriced either way.
devils_advocate.what_would_prove_it: The correct equipment-purchase line from the cash-flow statement substituted into the capex series, and the reverse DCF re-run. If corrected FCFF is materially negative — which is what a lessor growing its portfolio this fast should produce — the model is structurally inapplicable, not merely mis-parameterised.
devils_advocate.already_visible: Yes, and today it is no longer an inference. This morning the argument rested on the arithmetic implausibility of adding $161M of revenue in a year on $31M of equipment purchases. Today the 2026-08-25 8-K supplies a directly observed capital outlay: $262.9M paid at closing on 2026-08-24 for 12 aircraft and 13 engines, in a single transaction, roughly 8.5x the largest annual capex figure in the extract. The capex alias is not merely incomplete for this filer, it is missing essentially all of the spending. Corrected FCFF is far below $350M and, for a lessor buying $263M of assets in one deal while reserve revenue declines, plausibly negative. The counter loses.
devils_advocate.unresolved: I still could not read the 10-K to state the correct equipment-purchase figure — SEC egress is blocked from this runtime — so I can say the corrected base is far below $350M and plausibly negative, but not what it is. I also do not know how the $262.9M was funded, so I cannot say what the post-transaction debt load is against the $2.70B already outstanding, and that matters more than usual on a balance sheet at roughly 4x debt to equity.

what_changed: The one item left open by this morning's pass is now closed, and it settles the model question against the model. The 2026-08-25 item 2.01 8-K is the completion, on 2026-08-24, of a portfolio acquisition: Willis Dallas Ltd. purchased two target companies and their subsidiaries from WNG International Master Fund II, L.P. and WNG II Aircraft Management (Delaware), LLC, comprising 12 commercial aircraft and 13 aircraft engines, at a $379.3M base purchase price and an adjusted purchase price of approximately $262.9M paid at closing. Otherwise unchanged from this morning: the three-for-one forward stock split approved 2026-06-23, implemented 2026-07-17, trading split-adjusted from 2026-07-20; and Q2 2026 results on 2026-08-04 showing EPS of $1.31 against $2.81 and net income to common of $28.7M against $59.0M on lower short-term maintenance reserve revenue. Price $52.87, unchanged from this morning's screen.
consensus_case: The market prices an engine lessor in the second year of an aggressive portfolio build, at the moment its cycle has started to turn. Willis Lease grew revenue from $419M to $569M to $730M across the window, and it has not stopped: on 2026-08-24 a fully owned subsidiary closed the purchase of two target companies holding 12 commercial aircraft and 13 spare engines from WNG International Master Fund II, at a $379.3M base price and roughly $262.9M adjusted price paid at closing. That is a business consuming capital, not returning it, funded on $2.70B of debt against $662M of equity. Q2 2026 delivered the first material earnings decline of the cycle — EPS $1.31 against $2.81, net income to common $28.7M against $59.0M — driven by lower short-term maintenance reserve revenue as older engines saw reduced flying. A stock down 26% over 21 days is the market repricing a levered lessor whose reserve revenue has rolled over while it takes on another $263M of assets.
base_case_rationale: I will not supply one, because the FCFF base the growth rate would be applied to is not a real number. The screen reports a $350.2M base — roughly 48% of revenue — which no capital-intensive lessor produces. The cause is a capex alias that misses the entire category of spending this company exists to do, and today's 8-K makes that concrete rather than inferential: a firm that just paid $262.9M in cash for aircraft and engines in a single transaction cannot have had capital expenditure of $31.1M, $15.6M and $5.1M in the three preceding years, which is what the extract records. See the data-quality note. Applying any growth rate to that base would produce a fair value built on a number that is wrong by an order of magnitude.
key_risks: The +177.3% baseline gap and 93rd-percentile cohort rank are artifacts of the broken capex input and must not be treated as signal
